title: Security: WPA3 for Wi-Fi 7
summary: Wi-Fi 7 requires WPA3: why the bar is set there, and how a hospital can get ready.

opener.promise: Wi-Fi 7 makes WPA3 sign-in the price of entry
opener.problem: Many hospital devices and networks still sign in with WPA2, which Wi-Fi 7 does not use.

beats.heading: Wi-Fi 7 requires WPA3

caption.headline: Wi-Fi 7 requires [[wpa3|WPA3]]
caption.takeaway: Devices that sign in with [[wpa2|WPA2]] can’t use Wi-Fi 7{{wifi7-no-wpa2}}; WPA3 unlocks it.

beats.body:
Wi-Fi 7 comes with a security rule: a Wi-Fi 7 connection between a device and an [[access-point|access point]] signs in with [[wpa3|WPA3]], never [[wpa2|WPA2]] {{wifi7-no-wpa2}}. That holds for shared-password networks and for staff sign-in alike.

A device limited to WPA2 can still join a network that offers WPA2, but it connects without Wi-Fi 7 or multi-link {{wifi7-no-wpa2}} and stays out of the 6 GHz band {{wpa3-6ghz-required}}.
beats.bottomLine: To get Wi-Fi 7’s benefits, both the device and the network it joins need WPA3.
beats.sceneDescription: A hallway wall on a hospital unit with two doors under an access point labeled Wi-Fi 7: WPA3 sign-in. The infusion pump and the workstation each hold their own key. An older phone that supports only WPA2 is turned away from the main doors and moves to a smaller side door, a separate network for older devices. A note shows what the earlier generation accepted.

callout.title: The Wi-Fi 7 security rule
points: Wi-Fi 7 connections sign in with WPA3, not WPA2{{wifi7-no-wpa2}}
6 GHz has required WPA3 since Wi-Fi 6E{{wpa3-6ghz-required}}

questions.q: Will our older clinical devices still connect?
questions.a: Yes, if the network still offers WPA2 for them, through WPA3 transition mode or a separate network{{wpa3-transition-options}}. They stay off 6 GHz{{wpa3-6ghz-required}} and don’t get Wi-Fi 7{{wifi7-no-wpa2}} until they are updated or replaced.

cisco.text: A Cisco network offers Wi-Fi 7 only when its security meets the requirements; otherwise access points run it as Wi-Fi 6 or 6E{{cisco-noncompliant-downgrade}}. Devices that connect with WPA2 cannot use Wi-Fi 7 or multi-link{{cisco-wpa2-no-mlo}}.

beats.heading: Why Wi-Fi 7 requires WPA3

caption.headline: Why Wi-Fi 7 requires WPA3
caption.takeaway: One stronger sign-in on every band, as the Wi-Fi Alliance moves everyone to WPA3{{wfa-wpa3-whenever-possible}}.

beats.body:
**WPA3 is the industry’s direction.** WPA3 support has been required in new Wi-Fi CERTIFIED devices since 2020, it is mandatory in the 6 GHz band, and the Wi-Fi Alliance recommends it wherever possible {{wfa-wpa3-whenever-possible}}.

**One connection, every band.** A Wi-Fi 7 multi-link connection is a single connection across bands, with security coordinated across all of its links {{mlo-tid-mapping}}. The 6 GHz band already allows only WPA3 {{wpa3-6ghz-required}}, and Wi-Fi 7 applies the same rule to every Wi-Fi 7 connection {{wifi7-no-wpa2}}.

**It closes WPA2’s best-known gaps.** A recorded sign-in can no longer be cracked offline {{wpa3-sae}}, and staff devices must check they are on the real network, not a [[fake-access-point|fake access point]] {{wpa3-ent-cert-validation}}.
beats.bottomLine: Wi-Fi 7 raises the security floor, so every band and every Wi-Fi 7 device meets the same stronger standard.
beats.sceneDescription: A wide view of the hallway wall with both doors under the access point, labeled WPA3 on every band. At the keypad door, an outsider’s recorded sign-in turns into a sealed gray box with nothing to crack. At the staff door, the workstation checks a gold certificate seal before trusting the real access point, and both devices hold their own keys.

callout.title: Why WPA3, at a glance
points: Required in new certified devices since 2020{{wfa-wpa3-whenever-possible}}
One sign-in covers every band of a Wi-Fi 7 connection{{mlo-tid-mapping}}
Stops offline password guessing{{wpa3-sae}} and [[fake-access-point|fake access points]]{{wpa3-ent-cert-validation}}

questions.q: We already use WPA2-Enterprise. What do we gain from WPA3?
questions.a: Mandatory certificate checks{{wpa3-ent-cert-validation}}, and in Only mode protected control messages{{wpa3-ent-pmf-required}}. Your sign-in server and credentials usually carry over; devices and access points need WPA3 support.

questions.q: What about guest Wi-Fi with no password?
questions.a: Wi-Fi Enhanced Open encrypts each guest device’s traffic without a password{{owe-what}}, so an open network is no longer readable by anyone nearby.

beats.heading: Getting a hospital ready for WPA3

caption.headline: Getting the hospital ready for WPA3
caption.takeaway: Inventory devices, test, move what you can to WPA3, and plan for the rest{{wpa3-transition-options}}.

beats.body:
Start with an inventory: which clinical devices, phones and workstations support WPA3 and Wi-Fi 7, and which need a software update or the maker’s sign-off first. Keep wireless drivers current, and test with your own devices before changing a clinical network {{cisco-client-readiness}}.

Move WPA3-capable devices first. WPA3 transition mode lets WPA3 and WPA2 devices share one network; where older devices struggle with it, two separate networks are the alternative {{wpa3-transition-options}}. Retire the older network as devices are replaced, aiming for a network that runs WPA3 only {{cisco-full-wpa3-goal}}.
beats.bottomLine: Treat WPA3 as a planned migration with clinical engineering, not a switch you flip. It is one layer of a wider security program.
beats.sceneDescription: The hallway wall seen wide. The infusion pump and the workstation sign in with WPA3 through the main doors, each holding its own key, while an older phone uses the smaller side door for older devices, labeled to be retired as devices are replaced. A label above the pump reads inventory, test, migrate.

callout.title: A practical path
points: Inventory and test each device’s WPA3 and Wi-Fi 7 support{{cisco-client-readiness}}
Older devices: transition mode or a separate network{{wpa3-transition-options}}
Retire the older network; aim for WPA3 only{{cisco-full-wpa3-goal}}

questions.q: Can we just switch everything to WPA3 now?
questions.a: Not in one step. Some older devices have trouble even with transition mode{{wpa3-transition-options}}, so test with your own devices first{{cisco-client-readiness}}. Many clinical devices also need their maker’s validation before any security change.

questions.q: Does WPA3 make our network compliant?
questions.a: No single feature does. WPA3 is one layer of security; it complements network segmentation, device management and your organization’s security and compliance processes.

cisco.text: Cisco’s Wireless Configuration Analyzer Express checks controller configuration against the Wi-Fi 7 requirements{{cisco-wifi7-readiness-check}}. For older or sensitive IoT devices, Cisco guidance describes keeping a separate network alongside the WPA3 one{{cisco-legacy-iot-ssid}}.

lineage.lead: A separate Wi-Fi Alliance security program, not part of one generation.

sinceWifi6.wifi6: WPA3 becomes required for new Wi-Fi CERTIFIED devices{{wpa3-mandatory-cert}}.
sinceWifi6.wifi6e: In 6 GHz, no WPA2: WPA3, or Enhanced Open for guests{{6ghz-security-options}}.
sinceWifi6.wifi7: Every Wi-Fi 7 connection signs in with WPA3, on every band{{wifi7-no-wpa2}}.
